3. Now write a quick function that allows the user to easily query this API. The inputs to the function should be the title/subject to search for (string), a time period to search from (string - you’ll search from that time until the present), and an API key.

#Query NewsAPI and return the article data frame
query_news <- function(subject, from_date, api_key) {

  response <- GET(
    url = "https://newsapi.org/v2/everything",
    query = list(
      q = subject,
      from = from_date,
      language = "en",
      pageSize = 50,
      apiKey = api_key
    )
  )
  #Parse JSON response
  parsed_response <- content(
    response,
    as = "parsed",
    simplifyVector = TRUE
  )
  as_tibble(parsed_response$articles)
}

What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?

Long format data refers to multiple rows for each observational unit (e.g. recurring ID numbers for test scores such as math/reading)–this is generally the preferred format for statistical analysis because it is expected by many R functions from visualization libraries (ggplot2) to statistical modeling functions (lm/ANOVA/mixed effects models).
Wide format data generally has one row for each observational unit with different measurements separated by columns (e.g. one ID number followed by a math column and a reading column).

In order to access the previous folder in the working directory, the relative path you would specify to get the file would be “../myData.csv”. The notation “..” tells R to move up one folder or directory from “homework” into “myfolder”.
A major benefit of using R projects is that it is well suited to work with Git/Github. Another major benefit of using R is that all files associated with the project in one location.
Git is a version-control system that tracks changes made to files and allows us to view those very changes. It also manages branching and merging too. Github is the online platform that hosts Git repos and makes it easy to store, share, and even collaborate with others on projects.
Tibbles prints a finite amount of rows and columns such that it fits the size of the screen whereas a data.frame would display the whole dataset. Tibbles also have more strict notations that doesn’t allow partial column name matching.
